title: U.S. and China Set Up AI Hotline After Three-Day Summit
summary: What happens when the world's two biggest economies can't talk? Small problems can turn into big ones. That's why the U.S. and China spent three days in Washington, D.C., trying to keep the lines open. On Saturday, the two governments announced they will create a special channel for handling AI-related incidents and speed up work on military crisis communications. The summit between President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump didn't produce any giant breakthroughs, but analysts say the new working groups are important because they could stop disputes from escalating (getting worse). "Personal diplomacy between the two leaders is important, but the emphasis on working-level engagement, military-to-military dialogue and crisis-management mechanisms suggests an effort to make that stability more durable and institutionalized," said Wang Zichen of the Center for China and Globalization in Beijing. On trade, the two sides agreed to extend a truce on tariffs (taxes on imports) by two months and to keep reducing tariffs on about $30 billion worth of goods — mostly non-sensitive items like agricultural products and holiday decorations. China also agreed to import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the U.S. in 2027 and 2028. But Trump made it clear the U.S. won't slow down its AI work. "We're leading by at least a year, maybe a year and a half," he told reporters. "I would rather not integrate because we're leading by a lot." Both countries also said Iran should honor its promise not to develop nuclear weapons, and that no country should charge tolls on international waterways — likely a reference to the Strait of Hormuz. They will meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November.
why_it_matters: For teenagers who will live and work in a world shaped by AI and global trade, this summit shows how the two most powerful economies try to compete without tipping into conflict — the hotlines and working groups created now could set the rules for technology, jobs and prices for decades.

background_read: Hotlines between rival superpowers are not new: after the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, when the United States and the Soviet Union came close to nuclear war, the two sides set up a direct communications link so leaders could reach each other instantly instead of waiting on messengers.

Xi Jinping (China's president since 2013) and Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) have now held several rounds of face-to-face talks, and each meeting has produced a mix of small deals and unresolved disputes.

The two countries have been in a trade war since 2018, when both began placing tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of each other's goods — a fight whose higher prices reach companies and shoppers well beyond the two countries involved.

The summit statement about tolls on waterways almost certainly points to the Strait of Hormuz (the narrow channel between the Persian Gulf and the open ocean), which carries a large share of the world's oil exports.
APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) is a yearly forum of 21 economies around the Pacific, and this November's meeting will be in Shenzhen, a technology and manufacturing hub in southern China.

AI has become a central issue because both countries are racing to build the most powerful systems, and a mistake — a hacked network, a misread test, or a near-collision at sea — could grow serious fast without a direct channel for talking.

perspectives.description: The two governments created a channel for AI incidents and agreed to speed up military-to-military crisis communications, which lowers the odds that a mistake at sea or in cyberspace spirals into a real conflict. The analyst quoted calls this a step toward making stability 'institutionalized' rather than dependent on two leaders getting along.

There were no giant breakthroughs, tariffs on most goods remain in place, and the truce was extended only two months, so businesses still can't plan ahead. The hardest disputes — over advanced technology, security and territory — were left largely untouched.

During the Cold War, the U.S. and the Soviet Union set up a direct link after coming close to nuclear war. Summits like this one usually produce mechanisms that outlast the leaders who sign them, and their real value only shows up during a crisis — not in headlines.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — Shenzhen is the next test
perspectives.description: The next meeting is set for the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November. The open question is whether the AI and military talks keep meeting regularly, whether the coal and tariff commitments actually happen, and whether anyone can define what counts as an AI-related incident before one occurs.
